RE-APPROVED 2026-10-19, SUPERSEDING THE 132,024,417.53 APPROVED 2026-10-17. That figure was not wrong when it was signed: it was the shop default declared at the time, and this file's old note said so in as many words -- "UNQUALIFIED REVENUE IS SHOP REVENUE, by operator ruling". THE OPERATOR REVERSED THAT RULING ON 2026-10-18, in their own words recorded on `ontology/concepts/store.yaml`: "then it was aimed at simplicity ... now i am for correctnes and correct is that both internet and physical shops combined make revenue." 'Total sales in dollars' names no channel, so under the ruling nothing is assumed on the reader's behalf and it spans both. The figure is NOT a second decision -- it follows mechanically from the ruling, and it was re-derived by hand against contoso5.duckdb, not read back from the engine.
THE SQL IS SPELLED AS THE SUM OF THE TWO CHANNEL PARTITIONS ON PURPOSE. It is a different statement from the planner's single unfiltered SUM, so it still tests the engine against something other than itself, and it CARRIES THE PROOF OF THE RULING'S ARITHMETIC: the shop partition is 132,024,417.53167 -- the old approved figure, unchanged -- and the online partition is 86,790,054.12699, one store row, `store_key` 999999 named 'Online store'. The two partitions are disjoint and exhaustive and sum to this figure exactly. What the ruling admitted is that one row, and nothing else moved.
'IN DOLLARS' ASKS FOR NO CONVERSION, and that half of this reference is untouched by the ruling: the amounts are ALREADY USD. `CurrencyCode` records the currency the order was TRANSACTED in and the rate table converts USD -> local for display, so a dollar figure is the stored figure. Same value as ADV-22, which asks the same question in two words; STORE-09 is NO LONGER the same question, see its own note.

manual.note:
USD, NET, both channels, REVENUE FROM 2024 ONWARDS — the operator's window, 2026-10-23: "i actually meant from 2024 onwards". The warehouse ends 2025-12-31, so the window is 2024-01-01 to 2025-12-31.

REWORDED BY THE OPERATOR from "Revenue from new customers (first order in 2024) vs returning customers". The rewording names both cohorts by their FIRST ORDER DATE, which is what made the question answerable.

THESE TWO COHORTS DO NOT EXHAUST THE WINDOW, and that is stated here rather than left for a reader to find. A THIRD group exists: 4,865 customers whose first order was in 2025. They are neither "new with first order in 2024" nor "older than 2024", and they carry 10,257,871.11 of revenue inside the window. The question does not name them, so this answer does not include them — but any reading of these two figures as "the whole of 2024 onwards" is wrong by exactly that amount. THE CROSS-CHECK: 15,513,218.65 + 35,146,090.74 + 10,257,871.11 = 60,917,180.50 against the window's own net of 60,917,180.51, the cent being rounding applied once per cohort.

WHAT IT SHOWS. The 5,932 customers who arrived in 2024 brought 15,513,218.65 over two years — 2,615 each — while the 14,062 who were already customers brought 35,146,090.74, or 2,500 each. So a new customer is worth very slightly MORE per head over this window than an established one, and the established cohort's larger total is headcount rather than loyalty. A reading of this answer as "our old customers are more valuable" would be wrong.

AN EARLIER DRAFT SCOPED THE REVENUE TO 2024 ALONE (13,050,244.21 new against 18,589,446.72 returning) and had the attraction of partitioning that year exactly. The operator widened the window, which brings the 2025 cohort into existence and is why the remainder is disclosed above. CORRECTED 2026-10-23, AND THE ERROR WAS MINE, NOT THE ENGINE'S. The operator said "i actually meant from 2024 onwards" and that clarified the COHORT boundary — new customers are those whose first order is 2024 OR LATER. I attached it to the REVENUE instead, and wrote an expectation column named `net_2024_onwards` holding 5,932 / 15,513,218.65 and 14,062 / 35,146,090.74. Those figures answer a question nobody asked.
THE RULING GIVES ONE ANSWER AND THERE IS NO AMBIGUITY HERE. Operator, 2026-10-23: "the part of the question does not specify window which is older customer and onother part does. ruling says if no window is speicified take all periods, otherwise obey window." Applied: the COHORTS carry windows the question names — first order from 2024 onwards, first order before 2024 — so those are obeyed; the REVENUE carries none, so it covers all periods, by Order.period (C, operator ruling 2026-09-30), whose `never` forbids "any other window the question did not name".
THE COMPLETENESS CHECK THAT WOULD HAVE CAUGHT ME, and which I never ran: the two cohorts partition every customer who ever ordered, exactly once. 41.392 + 10.797 = 52.189, every customer with a sales line; 193.043.381,89 + 25.771.089,77 = 218.814.471,66, the bundle's entire net revenue. My wrong figures covered 19.994 of 52.189 customers and 50,7M of 218,8M, and broke that partition in a way one subtraction exposes.
THE WALK ANSWERED THIS CORRECTLY AND WAS GRADED WRONG TWICE, citing the rule in its own words: "an_unscoped_question_covers_all_time forbids narrowing the money to a window the question did not name". The engine read the declaration; the reference did not.
WHAT THIS QUESTION IS FOR, now that it is right: it is the corpus's test that the unscoped-period ruling is honoured on a measure whose COHORT is scoped — the one shape where a reader is most tempted to carry the cohort's window onto the money.
AND THE QUESTION'S OWN WORDS MOVED TOO, 2026-10-23, because correcting only the revenue repeated the very mistake it corrected. The wording said "first order IN 2024", which literally means calendar 2024 — 5.932 customers — while the operator's clarification and this expectation use 2024 ONWARDS — 10.797, including 2025's first-time buyers. The walk read the words and answered 5.932; it was right about the words. A clarification that lives in a note and contradicts the question is the same defect twice, so the question now says "from 2024 onwards" and the note records only WHY, not WHAT.

manual.note:
SUPERSEDED 2026-10-24 — SEE `reapproved` ABOVE. The paragraph below is the 2026-10-19 reasoning, kept because it is why this reference exists and because its argument against a FIGURE stands. APPROVED BY THE OPERATOR 2026-10-19: "3 refusals correct". A REFUSAL IS THE ANSWER HERE, and it is not a near miss or a partial credit -- it is the only correct reply. WHY A NUMBER WOULD BE WORSE THAN NO ANSWER: answering 0 says this is a population with nothing in it, when the truth is that it is not a population of this bundle at all. That difference is invisible in a figure and decisive to a reader, and it is the silent-wrong-answer class this whole plane exists to catch. THE STATEMENT BELOW PROVES THE ABSENCE and must keep returning NOTHING. That is what makes this reference checkable at all: there is no value to re-derive, but presence is a fact about the warehouse, so `check_reference_agrees_with_itself` runs it and fails if the bundle ever gains the thing the question names -- the direction in which an approved refusal goes stale in silence. AND THE REFUSAL MUST NAME THE TERM, which `expected_refusal_names` enforces. Refusals are not interchangeable: ADV-05 in this same corpus refuses with "self-score 0.40 is below the 0.50 threshold", which is the interpreter declining to read a question it did understand the shape of. Approving "it refused" would accept that too and grade the STAGE instead of the ANSWER. THERE IS NO `Electronics` CATEGORY IN THIS BUNDLE. The eight it has are Audio, Cameras and camcorders, Cell phones, Computers, Games and Toys, Home Appliances, Music, Movies and Audio Books, and TV and Video -- several of which a reader might reasonably call electronics, which is exactly why the engine must not pick one. The rest of the question is answerable (German stores resolve, as ADV-04 shows), so the refusal turns on this one unresolved term and the engine says so: "No product category named 'Electronics' in data/lookups/contoso5_category_name.lookup.csv".
WHY THIS REFERENCE DEMANDS MORE THAN THE REFUSAL THE ENGINE GIVES TODAY, added 2026-10-19 after the operator asked why a single pass is treated as sufficient: "if something responds that something doesn't exist here - then its the repsonsibility of an agent to check adn doublecheck". They are right, and this file as first written would have APPROVED the unhelpful answer.
THE MEASUREMENT THAT SETTLES IT. The near-miss ladder cannot see this case and not by accident: difflib scores 'electronics' at 0.455 against its best category ('Cell phones') and 0.545 against its best sub-category ('Televisions'), both far under the 0.80 NEAR_MISS_FLOOR. That is correct behaviour for the instrument -- 'Electronics' is not a MISSPELLING of anything, it is a SUPERSET of several of these, and edit distance has no access to that. So the system runs its two deterministic passes, finds nothing, and reports the exhaustion of its instruments as certainty. Compare 'Turkey', which scores 0.36 against its best country: the same score, a completely different situation, and no way to tell them apart from the number.
AND THE MODEL WAS NEVER SHOWN THE EIGHT CATEGORIES. Measured on the prompt as sent: not one of 'Cell phones', 'Home Appliances' or 'TV and Video' appears anywhere in its 36,764 characters. The word 'category' does. So the model was asked for a category value, given no values, and guessed a reasonable English word -- then the system refused it for not being in a list it had never been given, and the refusal did not print the list either. Every register in this bundle is small enough to show: 234 values over twelve registers, the largest 67.
WHAT IS APPROVED HERE IS STILL A REFUSAL. There is no Electronics revenue to report and picking a subset of categories would be the system making the reader's decision, which it must never do. What changes is that the refusal must DISCLOSE the population it checked against, per the estate's standing rule -- answer the whole range and disclose the narrower population, or ASK; never narrow silently -- and per the resolution ladder's own third rung, exact -> near miss -> ask with candidates. STORE-04 already reaches that rung and names all three of its columns, so the mechanism exists and simply is not wired to an unresolved VALUE.
THIS REFERENCE THEREFORE FAILS TODAY, deliberately. The engine refuses and offers nothing, so `expected_refusal_offers` is unmet. That is a measured gap with an owner rather than a silent one, which is the whole point of writing it down.

manual.note: SUPERSEDED 2026-10-24 — SEE `reapproved` ABOVE. The paragraph below is the 2026-10-19 reasoning, kept because it is why this reference exists and because its argument against a FIGURE still stands. APPROVED BY THE OPERATOR 2026-10-19: "3 refusals correct". A REFUSAL IS THE ANSWER HERE, and it is not a near miss or a partial credit -- it is the only correct reply. WHY A NUMBER WOULD BE WORSE THAN NO ANSWER: answering 0 says this is a population with nothing in it, when the truth is that it is not a population of this bundle at all. That difference is invisible in a figure and decisive to a reader, and it is the silent-wrong-answer class this whole plane exists to catch. THE STATEMENT BELOW PROVES THE ABSENCE and must keep returning NOTHING. That is what makes this reference checkable at all: there is no value to re-derive, but presence is a fact about the warehouse, so `check_reference_agrees_with_itself` runs it and fails if the bundle ever gains the thing the question names -- the direction in which an approved refusal goes stale in silence. AND THE REFUSAL MUST NAME THE TERM, which `expected_refusal_names` enforces. Refusals are not interchangeable: ADV-05 in this same corpus refuses with "self-score 0.40 is below the 0.50 threshold", which is the interpreter declining to read a question it did understand the shape of. Approving "it refused" would accept that too and grade the STAGE instead of the ANSWER. CONTOSO DOES NOT SELL IN TURKEY. The nine rows of `dim_country` are Australia, Canada, France, Germany, Italy, Netherlands, United Kingdom, United States and the 'Online' sentinel -- and no sale line in the bundle reaches a Turkish store or customer. 'Sales in Turkey were 0' would be a false sentence about a market that does not exist.

THE SAMPLING-DATE RULING REVERSED THIS ANSWER, and that is the whole content of this reference. Measured both ways on 2026-10-23:

On the clock the honest reply was "no" — and it was honest for the wrong reason. There are no sales in Q4 2026 because THE DATA STOPS ON 2025-12-31, ten months earlier, not because nothing was sold. A reader given "no" could not tell "we sold nothing this quarter" from "your question is past the end of the warehouse", and that is exactly the silent-wrong-answer class this plane exists to catch. It is the same distinction MQ-09 and MQ-13 hold for a missing country: False and a refusal are different facts wearing one word.
THE WINDOW IS DERIVED, NOT TYPED. The SQL above takes `MAX(order_date)` from the relation and truncates it to a quarter, so it re-derives the anchor on every run rather than carrying 2025-12-31 as a literal. That is the same canon the bundle's vintage records (`mac.canon.scoped_latest` on `Order.now_is_the_newest_order`), spelled inline here because a reference must be runnable on its own. When the warehouse grows, this oracle follows it and `tools/check_vintage_fresh.py` reports the drift against the recorded vintage.
THE ANSWER IS NOT JUST `true`, AND THE DISCLOSURE IS NOT OPTIONAL. A defaulted anchor obliges the answer to say what it covered — `mac_runtime.vintage.AsOfAnchor.disclosure` renders it and there is no flag that turns it off. The reply must carry: "Relative periods are anchored to 2025-12-31, this bundle's recorded vintage ... not today's date (2026-10-23)", and the window 2025-10-01 to 2025-12-31. A bare `true` with no window is the same defect as a bare `no`.

A case that separates those two readings needs an anchor mid-quarter and this bundle has none.

manual.note:
A COMPOUND QUESTION, AND THE SECOND HALF CANNOT BE ANSWERED. "how many store we have in france" has one answer; "in what cities are they" has none, and the right reply names that rather than substituting the nearest column.
THE COUNT. Trading premises whose own country is France, by the store's country rather than the customer's — "stores WE HAVE in France" is about where our shops stand. The declared `active` default supplies "currently", since the question names no past state. On this question the grains do not part company: every French site holds exactly one premises and none has ever closed, so premises, sites and trading all give the same figure. That is worth knowing, because it means a wrong answer here cannot be blamed on the store/location grain.
THE CITIES. `main.store` carries no city or town column; a store's finest place is its `state`, which in France means regions and overseas territories. `GeoAreaKey` identifies the site, not a geography. City exists in this bundle only as `dim_customer.city` — where a customer LIVES, not where a shop stands — and it is declared `offers.suppressed: DQ-IDENTIFYING-DIM_CUSTOMER-CITY`, so it may not appear in an answer even for customers.
SO THE CORRECT REPLY IS A FIGURE PLUS A NAMED GAP: the count, and that stores carry no city, with the regions offered instead if the reader wants them. Substituting regions SILENTLY is the failure this question is here to catch — it is the same move that once bound "internet business" to `Country = 'Online'`, the nearest register value available, and returned a plausible wrong figure.
WHAT THIS REFERENCE CANNOT GRADE, said plainly. `expected` holds one value and `expected_outcome` takes one outcome, so the format cannot express "answer this half, refuse that half". A walk that returns the count and says nothing about cities grades EXACT here, the same as one that returns the count and names the gap. The partial refusal is the thing worth measuring and it is not yet measurable — a gap in the acceptance format, not in the question.

REPHRASED BY THE OPERATOR 2026-10-23, verbatim: "compare revenue of customers (a) having purchaed before 31.12.2025 vs (b) having first purchased after 01.01.2024", and kept AS DICTATED after the overlap below was put to them — "as you wrote it, overlap and all". THE DATE WAS CORRECTED BY THE OPERATOR MID-WRITE: "sorry stop! / i think i made mistake / it is not 31.12.2025 but 31.12.2023". The 2025 version had been written and measured, and it put (b) almost entirely INSIDE (a) — 10,757 of (b)'s 10,782 customers were also in (a), because anyone who first bought in 2024 had of course purchased before 31.12.2025. With 2023 the two groups are DISJOINT BY CONSTRUCTION: a customer who purchased before 31.12.2023 has a first order no later than that date, so they cannot have FIRST purchased after 01.01.2024. Measured 2026-10-23: 0 customers in both.
(a) purchased before 31.12.2023 41,390 customers 193,042,649.52 (b) first purchased after 01.01.2024 10,782 customers 25,732,927.48 in BOTH 0 in NEITHER 17 customers 38,894.66
SEVENTEEN CUSTOMERS ARE IN NEITHER GROUP, and the figures are honest about it rather than rounded over: a customer whose FIRST order fell exactly on 31.12.2023 or 01.01.2024 fails both strict boundaries. So the two groups do NOT sum to the bundle — 41,390 + 10,782 = 52,172 of the 52,189 customers who ever ordered, and 193,042,649.52 + 25,732,927.48 = 218,775,577.00 of 218,814,471.66. The 38,894.66 difference is those seventeen. A run that returns a clean partition summing to the whole has widened one boundary to swallow them. THE BOUNDARIES ARE INCLUSIVE, RULED BY THE OPERATOR 2026-10-23: "i think this is conequence of calendar fucntions. model is right here". A DATE IN A QUESTION NAMES A DAY, NOT AN INSTANT, so "before 31.12.2023" and "after 01.01.2024" MARK the boundary rather than excluding it. Strict exclusion is a timestamp reading of a date literal, and the two dates here are ADJACENT — a person writing them is drawing one line, not leaving a one-day hole in the middle of it. WHAT MY STRICT READING COST, and I had written the defect in as if it were a feature. With `<` and `>` the two groups covered 41.390 + 10.782 = 52.172 of the 52.189 customers who ever ordered, and 218.775.577,00 of 218.814.471,66 — seventeen customers and 38.894,66 in neither group, because their FIRST order fell exactly on one of the two named days. This note then told the next reader that "a run that returns a clean partition summing to the whole has widened one boundary to swallow them", which framed the correct answer as the thing to catch. The walk answered inclusively, renamed its own groups to say so — "(a) purchased ON OR BEFORE 31.12.2023", "(b) first purchased ON OR AFTER 01.01.2024" — and was graded wrong for being right. SO THE TWO GROUPS NOW PARTITION EVERY CUSTOMER WHO EVER ORDERED, EXACTLY ONCE: 41.392 + 10.797 = 52.189 every customer with a sales line 193.043.381,89 + 25.771.089,77 = 218.814.471,66 the bundle''s entire net revenue That completeness is the check this reference exists to carry, and it is what the strict reading destroyed. WHAT IS OWED AND IS NOT THIS REFERENCE''S TO SETTLE: the inclusive reading of a named date is now a RULING with no declaration. Nothing in the bundle states it, so the next question written with "before <date>" depends on whoever authors it remembering this note. It belongs with the calendar family — the same gap that leaves age ROUNDING undeclared after the operator ruled "rounding BOTH, chosen at use" on 2026-10-16. THE EXPECTATION IS THE COUNTS AND THE FIGURES, WITH ORDER CARRYING (a) AND (b). Group (a) is row one, (b) is row two, and `ordered: true` is what makes a transposition fail. The group CAPTION is deliberately not checked, for the reason recorded on ADV-27: a caption is prose written by whoever composed the statement and no two authors spell it alike, while the figures are facts about the warehouse. manual.note:
REWORDED BY THE OPERATOR 2026-10-23, verbatim: "compare revenue in 2024 for customers odler then 2024 vs customers who first bought in 2024". It is the OTHER half of the pair with ADV-26, and between them they close the ambiguity ADV-11 carries. "REVENUE IN 2024" IS THE WINDOW, SAID FIRST AND SAID PLAINLY, which is the whole difference. Here the 2024 window qualifies the REVENUE for both cohorts; in ADV-26 it qualifies only the COHORT and the revenue is lifetime. The three figures a reader could get from one loosely-worded question are therefore all now pinned to a question that asks for exactly one of them: ADV-27 revenue IN 2024 old 18,589,446.72 new 13,050,244.21 ADV-11 revenue 2024 ONWARDS old 35,146,090.74 new 15,513,218.65 ADV-26 revenue LIFETIME old 193,043,381.89 new 15,513,218.65
AND NOTE WHAT THE OLD COHORT'S CUSTOMER COUNT DOES: 8,119 here against 41,392 in ADV-26. Both are "customers older than 2024" — the difference is that this question only counts the ones who BOUGHT AGAIN IN 2024, because a customer with no 2024 line contributes no 2024 revenue and so appears in no row. That is a property of the window, not a filter anyone added, and it is the thing most likely to be mistaken for an error. THE NEW COHORT'S COUNT IS 5,932 IN ALL THREE READINGS, because a customer whose first order is in 2024 necessarily has a 2024 line. Only the old cohort moves, which is why every one of these questions needs both rows to discriminate anything. "OLDER THAN 2024" IS READ AS FIRST ORDER BEFORE 2024-01-01 — the customer's relationship began earlier — and not as the customer's own record age: `dim_customer` carries `valid_from`, which is a different fact and would answer a different question. 2025's first-time buyers are in neither cohort. ACCEPTED 2026-10-23 — THE WALK'S ANSWER WAS RIGHT AND THIS REFERENCE WAS OVER-SPECIFIED. Operator, verbatim: "i accept this as corect ... semantically perfect !!!!". The walk returned two rows, in this order, with 18,589,446.72 and 13,050,244.21 — both figures exact — and was graded WRONG on a `customers` column (8,119 / 5,932) THAT THIS QUESTION NEVER ASKS FOR. I had volunteered it when writing the reference; an expectation is not the place to add columns the question does not request. SO THE EXPECTATION IS NOW THE TWO FIGURES, AND THE COHORT IDENTITY IS CARRIED BY `ordered: true`. Row 1 is the older cohort, row 2 the newer. That is deliberate and it is the honest shape: a cohort CAPTION — "older than 2024", "Customers who first bought before 2024", "Existing customers" — is prose written by whoever composed the statement, not a fact about the warehouse, and no two authors spell it alike. The FIGURES are the fact. Order is what distinguishes the two rows, and `ordered: true` is what makes a transposition fail. AND THE SQL RETURNS ONLY WHAT IS FILED, which it did not when this change was first made. I dropped the caption from `expected` and left it SELECTed, so the statement returned two columns against one filed and `oracles.py` correctly called the reference DEAD — a reference that does not reproduce its own answer, which is the one thing this plane may never contain. The cohort now lives in the GROUP BY and ORDER BY, where it decides which row is which WITHOUT being returned: row 0 is the older cohort, row 1 the newer, and that is what `ordered: true` checks. WHAT IS STILL CHECKED, so this is not a loosening into nothing: two rows and no more, in this order, each carrying its exact figure to the cent. Swap them and it fails; drop one and it fails; change either figure and it fails. What can no longer fail is a different wording of the caption.

manual.note:
THE OPERATOR'S OWN QUESTION, asked on 2026-10-22, and added to the deck at his instruction. It is here because it is the first question in this corpus whose SUBJECT is the declared populations themselves: `online` and `physical` are not a filter it happens to need, they are the two things being compared.
USD. 86,790,054.13 over 132,024,417.53 — the amounts in v_contoso5_sales_line ARE USD and must not be converted (currency.ambiguity.code_is_not_the_unit_of_the_amounts; `currency_code` is the currency TRANSACTED IN). Converting through ExchangeRate gives 0.6461, and a run without the declarations did exactly that.
NET, not gross. Gross gives 0.6567, units sold 0.7153, distinct orders 0.7150 and distinct customers 0.7789 — five defensible figures for one English sentence, which is why net_revenue.default.revenue_means_net says to answer with net_amount and SAY NET.
THE CHANNEL SPLIT IS THE DECLARED PREDICATE, not the store's name: Store's `physical` population is store_code <> -1 and `online` is = -1, from Store.channel. A reading that finds the online store by matching store_name = 'Online store' is right by luck.

manual.note:
ONE HALF OF A DELIBERATE PAIR, added 2026-10-23 with AGG-17. Together they test a single proposition: that the eight DECLINED answers in this corpus are ambiguous QUESTIONS rather than a model that cannot answer, and that naming the reading in the question recovers the answer.
WHAT THEY ARE SPLIT FROM. AGG-12 asks "What percentage of total net revenue comes from Germany?" and the walk refused it, in these words:

    "11.2601% if 'from Germany' means the customer's country (24,638,830.18 of 218,814,471.66);
     6.573% if it means the store's country (14,382,768.44 of 218,814,471.66).
     I will not choose between them."

That refusal is CORRECT and is not a failure. `Country.whose` declares three paths — store, customer, location — with their own surface names, and carries `never: pick between the store and the customer silently, and never average the two` (RULING-2026-10-22). AGG-12 names no path, so there is nothing to pick from. AGG-12 STAYS IN THE CORPUS UNCHANGED for exactly that reason: the ability to refuse an underspecified question is a capability worth a test of its own, and these two do not replace it.
WHAT THIS ONE ADDS is the word AGG-12 lacks: `customers resident in`, which is the declared `customer` path (`customer__based_in__country`, surfaces "customer country", "where our customers are"). So an answer of 11.2601 is evidence that a named path is followed, and an answer of 6.573 would be evidence that the naming was ignored — the two outcomes are distinguishable, which is the point of splitting rather than rewording in place.
THE DENOMINATOR IS BOTH CHANNELS AND ALL TIME: 218,814,471.66 over 2016-05-19 to 2025-12-31, by `revenue_means_both_channels` (ruled 2026-10-18, reversing an earlier shop-only reading) and `Order.period`. Only the NUMERATOR is filtered to Germany; a reader who filtered both would get 100%.

THE OTHER HALF OF THE PAIR added 2026-10-23 with AGG-16, and the more informative of the two. See AGG-16 for what the pair is testing and for the walk's refusal of AGG-12 in its own words.
WHY THIS SIDE IS THE DISCRIMINATING ONE. The customer reading, 11.2601, is also AGG-12's approved figure — so an agent that ignored the question's wording entirely and answered AGG-12's number would still pass AGG-16 by luck. It cannot pass THIS one that way: 6.573 is reachable only by taking the store path, which is the path `shops sited in` names (`store__trades_in__country`, surfaces "store country", "where we trade", "trading country"). A pair where only one half can be passed by accident is half a test; this is the half that carries the weight, and AGG-16 is there to show the same instrument answers both.
THE WEB SHOP IS WHY THE TWO FIGURES ARE SO FAR APART, and it is not a rounding story: the store path attributes a sale to the premises that rang it up, and the web shop is a sentinel row with no country, so 86,790,054.13 of online revenue falls out of every country on this path while staying in the denominator. Hence 14,382,768.44 of 218,814,471.66 = 6.573%, against 24,638,830.18 = 11.2601% on the customer path, which can place an online sale in a real country because the CUSTOMER has one. Both figures are correct about different things; neither is a better answer to AGG-12's wording, which is why that question is answered by refusing.
THE DENOMINATOR IS DELIBERATELY NOT NARROWED to physical sales. Dividing German shop revenue by physical-only revenue (132,024,417.53) gives 10.894% — a third figure, and a reasonable question, but not this one. This asks for a share of TOTAL net revenue, and `revenue_means_both_channels` (ruled 2026-10-18) fixes that total at both channels.
